core.now: Delivery failures are how attackers and misconfig hide.
core.why: If CloudTrail is not delivered, you have no account-level audit trail.

core.now: Treat CloudTrail disablement as an incident, not a config footnote.
core.why: StopLogging is an integrity attack on the same audit trail.

core.now: Ingest findings before you invent custom detections.
core.why: GuardDuty is AWS-native threat findings already scored for you.

core.now: Compliance and availability both fail when rules go NON_COMPLIANT.
core.why: Config drift is the control-plane change you did not intend.

core.now: Root is the break-glass identity; every use is an audit event.
core.why: Root account usage is never routine in a well-run account.

core.now: Privilege changes should be reviewed the same day they land.
core.why: IAM policy changes alter who can do what in the account.

core.now: High/critical findings need owners, not a dashboard of counts.
core.why: Severity analysis turns GuardDuty volume into a queue.

aws.hypothesis: AWS monitoring should start with CloudTrail integrity and delivery, GuardDuty, Config drift, and IAM/root—the controls AWS itself treats as the account security baseline—not incidental mentions of AWS in other products.
aws.label: Amazon Web Services

core.now: A spike in 802.1X failures is an outage, not a report.
core.why: Authentication failures are the first signal that users cannot get on the network.

core.m: Authentications per second versus licensed/SLO headroom
core.now: Capacity is a leading indicator for identity outages.
core.why: PSN TPS headroom tells you the pair will survive a node loss before it happens.

core.m: PSN sync lag and replication health codes 60100/60101
core.now: Unsynced nodes create un-debuggable allow/deny disagreements.
core.why: Replication lag splits policy: some PSNs authorize yesterday's rules.

core.m: Days to certificate expiry by role
core.now: Certificate expiry is scheduled pain you can still prevent.
core.why: Expired admin, EAP, or pxGrid certificates take the whole NAC plane down.

core.now: A saturated MnT or PSN looks like a network outage to users.
core.why: Node CPU, memory, disk, and threads are the health of the identity control plane.

core.m: pxGrid subscriber connectivity and topic health
core.now: A silent pxGrid drop breaks adaptive NAC without an obvious RADIUS clue.
core.why: pxGrid is how ISE shares session context with firewalls and EDRs.

core.m: Backup job success and operational-data backup age
core.now: An untested backup is discovered during the outage it was meant to cover.
core.why: Backups are the only recovery path after a PAN failure.

cisco_ise.hypothesis: ISE monitoring should start with whether people can authenticate, whether the cluster agrees with itself, and whether certificates and backups will survive the next failure—not with generic IPv6 or catch-all Cisco searches.
cisco_ise.label: Cisco ISE

core.m: Pods in CrashLoopBackOff and time in backoff
core.now: Workloads in backoff look Running on coarse dashboards.
core.why: CrashLoopBackOff is the kubelet saying a container never stays up.

core.m: Apiserver request latency by verb and resource
core.now: Slow apiserver precedes failed deploys and NotReady flaps.
core.why: API server latency is control-plane user experience for every kubectl and controller.

core.m: Nodes Ready=false and pods at risk
core.now: You need blast radius before default tolerationSeconds elapse.
core.why: Node NotReady starts the eviction clock for every pod on that worker.

core.now: Limit misses and MemoryPressure need different owners.
core.why: OOMKilled and eviction are memory-limit and node-pressure failures, not generic restarts.

core.m: Fluent Bit / Fluentd buffer overflow and retry exhaustion
core.now: Buffer overflow is a silent observability outage.
core.why: If the log pipeline is dropping, every cluster alert is flying blind.

core.now: Certificate expiry is scheduled and preventable.
core.why: Expired kubelet or apiserver certs take the cluster offline on a calendar.

core.now: Worker symptoms are downstream of control-plane loss.
core.why: Control-plane health (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) is the cluster itself.

kubernetes.hypothesis: Kubernetes monitoring should start with crashloop, apiserver latency, node NotReady, OOMKilled, the log pipeline, and certificates—the failure modes Kubernetes itself documents—not Docker-only OOM or incidental audit mentions.
kubernetes.label: Kubernetes

core.m: Average CPU used percent by host
core.now: Sustained high CPU becomes user-visible latency.
core.why: CPU saturation is the first host-level capacity signal.

core.now: Catch hosts before the kernel starts killing processes.
core.why: Memory pressure precedes OOM killer and swapping storms.

core.now: Full disks stop logging, databases, and packages at once.
core.why: Disk fill is a preventable availability failure on every Linux host.

core.now: Auth failures are both security and availability (lockouts).
core.why: SSH brute force is the default identity attack on Linux servers.

core.now: A crashed unit is an application outage with a host-local cause.
core.why: Systemd unit failures are service crashes on modern Linux.

core.now: Process kills without this signal look like random crashes.
core.why: OOM killer events are the kernel's last resort after memory pressure.

linux.hypothesis: Linux as a product means OS telemetry: CPU, memory, disk, authentication failures, and service crashes. HCI, ISE, or NGFW use cases that mention Linux in passing are out of this pack.
linux.label: Linux OS telemetry

core.m: Threat log count by severity and signature
core.now: Critical/high signatures are the SOC queue, not a weekly report.
core.why: Threat logs are the reason the firewall exists as a security control.

core.m: HA moved-to-active and HA1 heartbeat-loss events
core.now: The second failure after an unnoticed failover is an outage.
core.why: HA failover and HA1 loss leave the pair without a spare.

core.now: Log-forwarding gaps are silent until the next incident review.
core.why: If logs never reach Splunk, every other PAN-OS use case is dark.

core.m: Certificate inspection and untrusted issuer alerts
core.now: Certificate faults show up as user-visible SSL errors first.
core.why: Untrusted issuers and expiring decryption certs break inspection and VPNs.

core.now: Config drift on the dataplane is a change-control failure in production.
core.why: Panorama push failures mean the running policy is not the intended policy.

core.now: VPN down is a workforce outage.
core.why: GlobalProtect portal/gateway health is remote-access availability.

core.now: Policy that keys on user/group silently degrades to IP-only.
core.why: User-ID mapping failures make allow/deny decisions anonymous.

paloalto.hypothesis: PAN-OS monitoring should start with threat logs, HA health, log forwarding, certificates, and config-push failures. VMware or Fortinet titles that merely mention Palo Alto must not enter this pack.
paloalto.label: Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS

core.m: Datastore capacity used percent and days-to-full
core.now: Guests freeze when the datastore is full, often with no guest-level clue.
core.why: Datastore fill is the most common preventable VM outage.

core.now: Guest CPU looks fine while applications wait on pCPU.
core.why: CPU ready time is the hypervisor telling you VMs are queued, not busy.

core.m: Snapshot count and age per VM
core.now: Forgotten backup snapshots are a silent capacity leak.
core.why: Snapshot sprawl burns datastore space and slows storage.

core.now: If vCenter is sick you cannot manage HA, DRS, or alarms.
core.why: vCenter health is the control plane for every other vSphere signal.

core.now: You need remaining-host capacity and hardware root cause immediately.
core.why: HA failover means a host died and VMs restarted elsewhere.

core.now: Latency pages earlier than fill for I/O-bound estates.
core.why: Datastore latency is the storage path before capacity is exhausted.

core.now: Age, not count, tells you which disks to consolidate first.
core.why: Aged snapshots are the actionable follow-up to snapshot sprawl.

vmware.hypothesis: vSphere monitoring should start with datastore space, CPU ready, snapshots, vCenter health, and HA failovers—the signals VMware operators use to keep guests running—not every HCI neighbour that mentions a VM.
vmware.label: VMware vSphere
